verdict.rationale: Both changes implement the refund the same way: same handler structure, same status check, the cap set at amountPaid minus amountRefunded, and the same `Order.recordRefund`. Both are correct and well scoped. A's tests do more to protect the new input rules. They cover null, zero, negative and too-precise amounts and check that the stored refund stays unchanged. They also test a full refund and that refunding exactly the amount paid succeeds when it is lower than the total. B checks only a zero amount. B's tests do use the voucher (paid less than total) setup throughout, and its README row keeps the table aligned.
a_issues: The new README table row is longer than the column width, so the table's alignment breaks.
The report does not explicitly say which command was run to verify the 29 passing tests.
b_issues: Invalid-amount tests cover only zero; null, negative and too-precise amounts are left untested for the new command.
The refund-on-delivered test does not assert the amountRefunded value.

verdict.rationale: Both handlers are essentially the same and correct: same status check, same cap at amountPaid minus amountRefunded, same Validator reuse and same `recordRefund` on Order. B's tests are somewhat stronger. They check null, negative and too-precise amounts, and a full refund on a delivered order. Its paid-less-than-total test checks both the rejected 80.01 and the accepted 80.00. B's error message also says what was paid and what was already refunded. A's tests are solid but leave a few edge cases out, so B wins narrowly.
a_issues: Invalid-amount coverage only tests zero, not null, negative or more than two decimals.
Every test uses the same paid-less-than-total setup, so there is no full refund of a fully paid order.
b_issues: The new README table row is wider than the header columns, which breaks the table's alignment.
The over-refund error message is a bit long, though it is informative.
